definitions.definition: Artificial satellite that relays and amplifies radio telecommunication signals so two points on the ground can communicate.
Each orbiting body travels along an ellipse with its primary body at one of the two foci.
A line joining an orbiting body to its primary sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the body moves faster when closer.
The square of an orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, for all bodies orbiting the same primary.
Measure of how stretched an elliptical orbit is, from zero for a perfect circle toward one for a very elongated shape.
Circular equatorial orbit about 35,786 km above Earth's surface in which a satellite appears fixed in the sky to ground observers.
Deviation from a simple two-body orbit caused by forces such as a non-spherical central body, third bodies or atmospheric resistance.
Highly elliptical orbit with its low point near low Earth orbit and its high point at geostationary altitude, used as a stepping stone to the final orbit.
High-thrust rocket that lifts a satellite toward its transfer orbit, then releases it and usually falls back through the atmosphere.
Main body and structural component of a spacecraft that holds the payload, instruments and the supporting subsystems.
Steering of a spacecraft's orientation relative to a reference, using actuators and algorithms guided by sensor data.
Method of holding a spacecraft's orientation by spinning it, so its rotating mass resists disturbances.
Method of holding a spacecraft in a fixed orientation without rotation, using thrusters, reaction wheels or similar actuators.
Electrically driven rotor on a spacecraft axis that exchanges angular momentum with the vehicle in order to rotate it.
Gathering of measurements at distant locations and automatic transmission to receiving equipment where they can be monitored.
Counterpart of remote measurement, for systems that must receive outside instructions and data in order to operate.
Part of a spacecraft bus that generates, stores and distributes electrical power.
Series of interconnected units that forms a communications channel between a satellite's receiving and transmitting antennas.
Design in which the satellite itself demodulates, decodes, re-encodes and remodulates the signal, improving quality and allowing digital processing.
Accounting of all power gains and losses a signal experiences from transmitter to receiver, used to confirm adequate reception at design time.
Safety allowance between the received power and the receiver's minimum required power.
Loss of signal strength through empty space, depending on the ratio of distance to wavelength and roughly 20 log10(4*pi*d/lambda) dB.
Power a theoretical equal-in-all-directions antenna would need to produce the same peak signal strength as the real antenna in its strongest direction.
Ratio of an antenna's peak signal strength to that of a chosen reference antenna; meaningless without a stated reference.
Temperature of a resistor that would produce the same available noise power per unit bandwidth as the component or source considered.
Total of the antenna's noise temperature and the effective noise temperature of the receiver and its transmission lines.
Ten times the logarithm of the noise factor, which is one plus the equivalent noise temperature divided by 290 K.
Effective input noise temperature of amplifier stages in series: first-stage value plus later stages each divided by preceding gain, so early stages dominate.
Channel access method that lets several users share a channel by splitting its bandwidth into separate frequency sub-channels, one per user.
Channel access method letting several users share one frequency channel by taking turns, each transmitting in its own slice of time.
Unused gap at the end of a time slot that keeps one transmission from spilling into the next slot.
Repeating block of a data stream divided into time slots, each assigned to a different user.
Channel access method letting several transmitters share one frequency band by spreading their signals with a unique code each.
Pseudo-random chip sequence, running at a much higher rate than the data, combined with the data to widen its bandwidth.
Technique that widens a signal's bandwidth far beyond its minimum requirement, improving security and resistance to jamming.
Ratio of data bit time to chip time, which helps determine how many users a base station can support.
Mutually uncorrelated codes assigned to users in synchronous systems, which therefore do not interfere with one another.
Terrestrial radio station that communicates with spacecraft, transmitting to and receiving radio waves from them.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Dish-shaped antenna that is the principal telecommunications device of a ground station.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Ground facility that mainly receives telemetry, follows space missions or tracks satellites not in geostationary orbit.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Hub that links a satellite network to a terrestrial telecommunications network such as the Internet, offering uplink and broadcast services.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Orbit around Earth with a period of 128 minutes or less and eccentricity below 0.25, reaching up to about 2,000 km altitude.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Orbit roughly 2,000 to 35,786 km up from which satellites stay visible for 2 to 8 hours and cover wider areas than low-orbit ones.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Large group of low-orbit satellites needed for continuous coverage because each sees only a small part of Earth at once.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Slowing of low-orbit satellites by thin gas in the upper atmosphere, which makes orbits below 300 km decay quickly without re-boosting.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Signal round-trip time of about 240 ms from the equator through a satellite at that altitude, which hurts latency-sensitive uses such as voice.
definitions.unitTitle: Earth Station Technology and LEO/GEO Systems

definitions.definition: Satellite-based navigation system owned by the U.S. government that gives receivers their location and time wherever signal quality allows.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Calculation of a receiver's three-dimensional position from its distances to several satellites, derived from signal travel times.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Deviation of a receiver's own clock from satellite time, which is why a fourth satellite is needed to solve for it.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Data each satellite broadcasts at 50 bits per second, carrying transmission time, orbit information and constellation status.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Civilian ranging sequence of 1,023 chips sent at about 1 Mchip/s, so it repeats every millisecond.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Military precision sequence, much longer and faster than the civilian one and scrambled with a secret sequence to block spoofing.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Process of time-aligning a receiver-generated copy of a satellite's code with the incoming signal to find when a code point arrived.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Method that improves satellite positioning by applying corrections from nearby fixed ground stations, reducing error from several metres to a few centimetres.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System

definitions.definition: Adjustment applied to raw satellite-distance measurements before the receiver computes its position.
definitions.unitTitle: Satellite Navigation and the Global Positioning System
